claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled low-temperature aging will improve the combined strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance of high-entropy alloys relative to conventional homogenization routes.
Conventional homogenization produces a coarse-grained high-entropy alloy with a relatively uniform or suboptimal precipitate distribution.
Severe plastic deformation by high-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing can produce significant grain refinement in the alloy.
Controlled low-temperature aging after severe plastic deformation can induce fine, dispersed secondary precipitates.
The proposed processing sequence can establish a non-uniform precipitate distribution constituting a gradient microstructure.
The method is expected to work in high-entropy alloys whose elemental mixing supports metastable-phase formation and rapid precipitation kinetics.
Rapid recrystallization may prevent the proposed method from providing the expected benefits.
Over-aging can produce coarse precipitates and cause the proposed benefits to vanish or reverse.
Insufficient deformation can cause inadequate grain refinement and eliminate the proposed benefits.
The treatment will produce a dual-scale microstructure containing ultrafine grains at boundaries and dispersed nanoscale precipitates in the matrix.
Ultrafine grains and nanoscale precipitates jointly impede dislocation motion.
The proposed dual-scale microstructure deflects propagating cracks.
Grain refinement increases strength through the Hall–Petch effect.
Nanoscale precipitates enhance ductility and fracture resistance by impeding dislocation motion and crack initiation.
A graded microstructure improves local stiffness and load transfer, causing Young’s modulus to approach theoretical or design values.
The treated alloy will have approximately 15–25% higher yield strength than the conventionally processed baseline.
The treated alloy will have approximately 10–15% greater ductility than the conventionally processed baseline.
The treated alloy’s Young’s modulus will be within 10% of target design values.
The treated alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in fracture toughness relative to conventional processing.
Alloys prone to phase separation may not exhibit the proposed synergistic mechanical-property improvements.
